description: Working on the astronaut health monitoring challenge at the Gold Coast event. My background is in computing and medicine. Open to teammates with any skills.
summary:
Astronaut Health Twin is a visual tool that helps a crew member on a long mission keep watch over their own health. The challenge says it plainly: on long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in themselves. Most of those changes are slow, such as bone loss, a tired heart, short sleep or low mood, and a busy crew member who is not a doctor can miss them.

The tool gathers a person's health data in one place, with their body at the centre. It starts with the routine readings: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood. It keeps your own history, so each new reading is set against your own normal and against a published clinical chart. Then it shows you in plain words how you are doing today, what has changed, what to do now, and who to tell: yourself, the crew medical officer, or Earth.

It is built for prevention. A reply from Earth can take up to 20 minutes one way at Mars distance, so the first judgement has to happen on board. Many of these readings are already taken on today's spacecraft, on separate devices. What is missing is one quick answer drawn from all of them, for the person they belong to.

This is a concept prototype with simulated data. It is not a medical device and it does not diagnose. It builds on NASA's own work on medical support for crews far from Earth.
details: THE PROBLEM The space environment wears the body down slowly. NASA names five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity, and a closed environment. They can lead to the things everyone wants to avoid, such as bone loss, heart events, immune changes and behavioural health problems. On a long mission the astronaut has to notice these changes in themselves, and help from Earth is slow. THE IDEA One tool, with the body at the centre, that does three things the challenge asks for: gather, evaluate, act. Gather. The tool collects everything about one person in one place, and as much of it as possible arrives by itself. Nothing here needs a new sensor. Every source I found is in use, tested in orbit or in development: - Heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and skin temperature from a smart shirt (first used on the space station in 2019). - Sleep, activity and light from a wrist sensor (used in NASA's standard crew measurements since 2018, and in the Artemis II study of crew sleep and activity). - Blood sugar from a continuous glucose monitor (tested in orbit on a private mission in 2025). - Blood, saliva and urine results (samples are taken on the station today, and an on-board analyser flew there in 2019). - Radiation exposure so far (instruments that measure it are on the station, and a continuous one is in development). - Mood, symptoms and photos, which come from the crew member. I found no automatic mood sensor in use. Evaluate. Each reading is set against your own normal and against a published clinical chart, and shown on a body figure with a colour, a plain sentence and a trend over time. Two parts of this are concept and not yet built. The first is a normal that the tool learns from each person's own growing record, so it gets sharper the longer the mission runs. The second is one number that sums up the day. It would follow the biggest change, never the average, so five calm readings cannot hide one bad one, and it would always come with its reason. Act. The tool turns the readings into an ordered plan, soonest first. NASA's pages describe daily habits as the main protection in space: exercise, sleep and light, food, rest. So the plan points at the habit to change. Showing whether the change worked is concept, not yet built. Urgent findings show at once on the crew member's own device. Routine data goes back to Earth in batches, in one complete report, because a reply takes time. The tool never names a medicine and never says anyone is fit or cleared. Its rules are my own example, not NASA's and not medical advice. The astronaut owns it. A 2001 National Academies report found that astronauts can be reluctant to report symptoms, for fear of losing a flight. So readings are private to the crew member first, and only serious findings go to the crew medical officer and to Earth. EVERYTHING THE CHALLENGE LISTS IS INCLUDED - A body figure with four clickable regions (head, heart, core, arm), as a picture and as a 3D model. - Different places: spacecraft, station, rover and base. The place is filled in from the flight day of a simulated mission plan, so nobody is asked, and it can be changed by hand. - Prompts to take a measurement. A countdown starts by itself on the page when the plan asks for a re-check, shown at demo speed. - A check streak with three badges, counted over the sample week. It rewards taking the checks and never the numbers. - Charts that show each reading over time. - Colour coding to read a status at a glance. - Simple explanations: why each reading is checked, whether it can be taken in space, and how to use the page. WHY IT IS REALISTIC NASA says the space station today has a collection of separate medical devices, and it is studying whether one integrated system would serve future missions better. A 2026 review of AI for space healthcare concludes that AI is most plausibly one part of an integrated on-board system joining wearables, records, imaging, radiation monitoring and decision support, and it names personal baselines and small on-board models as near-term priorities. This project follows that direction. The parts exist. The new work is joining them and showing the result to the crew member. WHAT IS BUILT TODAY, AND WHAT IS CONCEPT Built and working in the prototype: the six readings with a body figure, colour labels, trends, the ordered plan, daily habits from NASA's pages, the place, prompts and reminders, the check streak, a photo, a look ahead, and a draft report for Earth. All readings are simulated. Concept, not yet built: a normal that is learned from your own record, the single change score, radiation and blood test inputs, the check on whether a habit worked, and an on-board AI model. WHAT IT BUILDS ON NASA has worked on this for years. Its Medical Data Architecture project built ground prototypes. Its clinical decision support work produced requirements and a concept. A 2020 NASA dashboard concept aims at helping crews diagnose and treat themselves. A 2025 proof of concept with Google supports a crew medical officer or flight surgeon. Teams on the ground already have software that shows crew health data. In what I could find, there is no finished tool that does this job for the crew member with routine readings and a personal record. This project is a small working demonstration of that part. HONEST LIMITS This is a concept prototype with simulated data. It is not a medical device, and it does not diagnose or clear anyone. The plan's rules were checked by AI reviewers, not by a flight doctor. The clinical chart for blood pressure and temperature, NEWS2, was made for hospital patients. The act-now lines for pulse, low blood sugar and mood are my own. No open dataset of astronaut readings was found, so nothing here has been trained or tested on real crew data. HOW IT WAS BUILT Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It runs in the browser with no server and no account, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. The rules live in their own files with automated tests. The 3D figure uses three.js. The code and tests were written with help from Claude (Anthropic). WHAT I HOPE TO ACHIEVE That a crew member with no medical training can see which change matters, what to do first and who to tell, early enough for a small change to fix it.
